## Teaching points

1. Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis: skin or mucosal signs with respiratory compromise or hypotension minutes after a new drug meet WAO criteria, and treatment must not wait for tryptase or allergy testing.
2. IM epinephrine (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh is first-line; repeat it after 5 minutes if there is no improvement. Antihistamines, steroids and bronchodilators are adjuncts only.
3. Persistent respiratory or cardiovascular compromise despite two IM doses is refractory anaphylaxis: start an IV epinephrine infusion with expert help.
4. Symptoms can recur within hours without re-exposure (biphasic reaction); a severe initial reaction and needing more than one epinephrine dose are risk factors and justify longer observation.
5. Severe reactions can follow a first known dose in a non-atopic patient; discharge with epinephrine autoinjectors, training, an action plan, trigger avoidance and allergy referral, and send a tryptase level when available.
